newsitem.title: CANADA: Ontario posts lower '96-97 deficit, trims taxes.
newsitem.headline: Ontario posts lower '96-97 deficit, trims taxes.

text.p: Ontario Finance Minister Ernie Eves on Tuesday made the following forecasts in the 1997/98 budget: Figures in billions of Canadian dollars.
Revenues 49.1 48.4 48.8
Expenditures 56.6 54.3 52.9
Program spending 45.3 42.4 40.9
Public debt charges 8.7 9.2 9.6
Deficit 7.5 6.6 4.8
Total debt 101 102 108
Ttl financial requirement 7.2 15.2
GDP pct 2.0 3.2 3.2
CPI inflation pct 1.6 1.9 1.9
Job growth pct 1.5 1.6-2.4 2.5-3.6
Unemployment rate pct 9.1 8.4-8.7 7.9-8.6
3-month Cdn T-bill rate 4.2 4.0 4.7
10-yr Cdn bond rate 7.2 7.4 7.3

Ontario's Conservative government delivered a lower than forecast deficit and a tax cut in its second full budget on Tuesday, but said it remained on track to balance the budget of Canada's most populous province by the turn of the century.
Eves revised Ontario's 1996/97 deficit to C$7.5 billion from a February forecast of C$7.67 billion.

"Our Balanced Budget Plan will ensure that the deficit is eliminated by the year 2000-01," Eves said in a speech prepared for delivery to the provincial legislature. "We have turned the corner toward a balanced budget," he said.
He said the government also would continue to cut personal income taxes during the 1997/98 fiscal year. Eves cut taxes by 15.5 percent in last year's budget.
He said on Tuesday the total tax cut would be 22.4 percent by January 1, 1998. The government has promised to reduce income taxes by 30 percent by 1999.
Eves said the 1997/98 tax cut would mean a drop to 47 percent from 49 percent of federal income tax effective July 1 and would be followed by an additional cut to 45 percent on January 1, 1998.
"This means that Ontario's rate of income tax will have been reduced by 22.4 percent since 1995," Eves said.
Eves said the budget deficit was projected to fall to C$6.6 billion in 1997/98 and drop to C$4.8 billion in 1998/99 on its way to zero in 2000-01.
He said the province expected its financial requirements to rise to C$15.2 billion in 1997/98 from C$7.2 billion in 1996/97.

Program spending will fall to C$42.4 billion in 1997/98 from C$45.3 billion in 1996/97, but less than forecast in last year's budget, which projected 1997/98 program spending to drop to C$40.8 billion.

Eves also unveiled a child care tax credit for families of two children or more with an income of up to C$40,000. Critics have attacked Ontario's budgets for cutting too deep into the social fabric of the province,
For business, Eves announced that the government would help with the creation of Community Small Business Investment Funds.

He said the government planned to introduce legislation to make the funds eligible for investment by Labor Sponsored Investment Funds. It also would allow major Canadian banks to earn back up to 75 percent of a surtax imposed in last year's budget for small business financing.
